title: Listening hard to reissued records
summary: Smithsonian reissues; one record a month played eight hours a day.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I thank you so much for saying that because I think this is what young people should know from someone like you who's been through the whole bit. And your sincerity about music, your sincerity about your teaching, your spreading your musical gospel to young people and being faithful to your craft, to know that you say -- all generations and all history, all the things that have been our history. Once you study the history of music of great players, read these books as you
mentioned, by these great writers, research the great players, and telling them, you can't very well get into something unless you know what preceded you.
And then listen to the players. The Smithonian Institute has a great selection of records.
I just found that out. They've got a lot of Armstrong records that got broken and I don't have any more, and I understand they reissued them.
I've got to remember to write a letter about that.
Yeah, I'm sure you'll enjoy them because they're just marvelous. And they go right back through it, Louis and Diz and everybody. And for young players, I would suggest very much that they get those.

Yeah, I think the young player should not only listen to the records, but don't, you know, just put them on while you're doing your homework or something -- that's all right, too, while you're walking around the house. But I mean, sit down and listen to these records and make them a part of yourself.
Like when you and I started out, I would maybe get one record a month. And I would play that record eight hours a day. And in a way I feel luckier because I know 150
Armstrong records, I could sing every part on the record -- unfortunately, many parts I wish I couldn't.
But I can sing them all. And I bet I know at least 100, 150 Ellington records the same way. I even tried to score out parts, you know, figure out on the piano what he was doing.
